column2: One who remembers or recites all these holy places is freed from all sins and goes to the city of Shiva and Vishnu.
At Bhanu-tirtha especially, bathing grants success in all aims; in that holy place of great merit there are a hundred holy places.
Having reported that task, when it was done, he came again, taking the mountain, to the divine mountain.
Bring that herb, place it on his heart, remembering Hari; then this noble-minded one will obtain all he desires.
As he went swiftly, the Vishalyakarani fell again on the Gautami's bank, where Hari, lord of yogis, is.
Show that herb quickly to me, father, without delay; there is nothing better in the three worlds than relieving another's pain.
Vibhishana said "So be it" and showed it to his son; his son cut a branch of the tree "Ishe tva" (and gave it), out of love also to the merchant; the good delight in others' welfare.
On this mountain where it fell, that tree is mighty; take its branch and place it on his heart; merely on touching it he will regain his own form.
Hearing his father's word, the noble-minded Vaibhishani did so properly and placed the piece of wood.
On his heart the merchant became possessed of eyes and hands; no one understands the power of gems, mantras and herbs.
Taking that very wood and remembering dharma alone, after bathing in the Gautami Ganga and bowing to Hari, lord of yogis,
the merchant went off again with the piece of wood, wandering to a city of a king, the great city, so it is heard.
A mighty king there was famed as Maharaja; he had no son, only a daughter who had lost her eyesight.
She was his only child, and his vow was thus: whether god or Danava, Brahmin or Kshatriya,
Vaishya or of Shudra birth, with or without qualities, to him this daughter was to be given who would bring back her eyes,
along with the kingdom. The king proclaimed this day and night. The merchant, hearing the proclamation, said:
I shall surely bring back the king's daughter's eyes.
They quickly took that merchant and presented him to the great king; by mere touch of that wood the king's daughter had eyes.
Then the astonished king said, "Who are you?" and the merchant told the king everything as it happened:
By the grace of Brahmins, by dharma and austerity, by the power of gifts and sacrifices with abundant fees, and by the power of a divine herb is my ability thus.
Hearing the merchant's words the king was amazed.
Ah, he is greatly powerful, likely a god; otherwise how is such ability seen in another? So I shall give him that daughter along with the kingdom.
Deciding thus in mind, he gave the daughter and the kingdom, and went off at will to wander, finding great distress.
Without a friend, no kingdom, no happiness; the merchant's son thought constantly of that very Brahmin.
This is the mark of the well-born among embodied beings on earth: their minds are always compassionate even toward those who harm them.
The great king went to the forest; that king Manikundala ruled the kingdom. Once, seeing the Brahmin Gautama,
whose wealth had been robbed by sinful gamblers, Manikundala, knower of dharma, took that Brahmin friend and honoured him.
He told him fully of the power of dharma and had him bathe in the Ganga for the removal of all his sins.
Surrounded by that Brahmin, all his own kin, merchants born in his own country, and the Brahmin's relatives,
and by chiefs such as the old Kaushika, near that lord of yogis he performed sacrifices, worshipped the gods, and then attained heaven.
From then on they know that holy place as Mritasanjivana, and Chakshus-tirtha with the Lord of yogis, giving merit even by remembrance, producing serenity of mind and destroying all evil thoughts.
Having conquered his enemies he quickly went to Indra's world, surrounded by gods; there he saw the lord of gods with the Maruts, Narada.
Pramati, bull among Kshatriyas, laughed at Indra, who was holding dice; seeing him laugh, Hari said to Pramati:
In the gods' abode, greatly wise one, enough of the Maruts' games; you have conquered the directions and reached heaven; play with me.
Hearing Hari's slightly angry words, King Pramati said "So be it" to Indra: "What wager do you consider?" Hearing Pramati's words, the king of gods said to the king:
Urvashi alone is our wager, who is to be won by all sacrifices.
Hearing Indra's words, the proud Pramati said, "I regard Urvashi as the wager; what do you think, king?"
What you say, lord of gods, Shatakratu, I accept. Pramati said to Indra likewise: "For my wager, my right hand, with armour and arrows, lawful, give; we shall play."
Having made this agreement, the two sat down to play; Pramati won there Urvashi, the goddess; having won her, Pramati in his fury said to Shatakratu:

Another wager for me, lord, afterwards in the game with you:
brahmapuran:171:12	the thunderbolt fit for gods, the victorious, with its excellent chariot; with that I shall play, king, with my hand, without hesitation.
Taking the dice and other jewel-adorned things, Pramati said, laughing, to Shakra, "I have won."
In the meantime a master of dice came there, Narada: the lord of Gandharvas, famed as Vishvavasu.
With Gandharva knowledge, king, I shall play with you. Saying "So be it," the king then said, "I have won."
Having defeated them, the king in folly spoke abusively to Devendra:
Neither in battle nor in play can you ever defeat me, Mahendra; therefore be my attendant. Tell me by what means your lordship over the gods came about.
Then in pride he said to Urvashi, "Go, be a servant." Urvashi said: "As I behave among the gods, so I shall behave toward you; you ought not to scorn me."
Pramati then said to her, "There are maidservants like you; why are you ashamed, fair one? Go, be a servant."
Hearing the king's words, the lord of Gandharvas, famed as Chitrasena, mighty son of Vishvavasu, said:
I shall play with you, king, for all of this, king, the kingdom, my life, and yours too.
Saying "So be it," the two best of kings, Chitrasena and Pramati, played again, enraged; Chitrasena won then.
Then with great Gandharva nooses he bound the king; Chitrasena won everything, with Urvashi foremost among the stakes,
the kingdom, treasury, army, and whatever other wealth there was; Pramati's wealth became Chitrasena's.
His young son said vigorously to the priest, the greatly wise Madhuchchhandas, son of Vishvamitra:
What sin was done by my father, and where is the greatly intelligent one bound? How will he return to his place and be freed from the nooses?
Hearing Sumati's words, the best of sages meditated, and Madhuchchhandas then told of Pramati's conduct:

Your father is bound in the world of the gods, great-minded one; through the many faults of gamblers he lost his kingdom.
brahmapuran:171:29	Whoever goes to a gambling hall is a sharer in trouble. Gambling, drink, meat and the like are vices, prince,
brahmapuran:171:30	which always arise among sinners as sinful in nature; each one alone leads to misfortune, sin and hell.
brahmapuran:171:31	Even the well-born become defiled by riding, sitting and talking with those who practise gambling; what then of the gambler himself?
brahmapuran:171:32	The wife of a gambler is always tormented, and the sinful gambler himself is tormented on seeing a woman.
brahmapuran:171:33	Seeing her, joyless, the sinner always says, 'Ah, in this wheel of worldly existence there is no sinner like me.'
brahmapuran:171:34	He has no pleasure born of objects in the world; no gambler is seen happy in either world.
brahmapuran:171:35	He always looks as if his mind were burnt by shame; without dharma, joyless, swallowed by pride, he wanders.
brahmapuran:171:36	A livelihood without gambling is praised for the twice-born: agriculture, cattle-keeping, trade; but he should not gamble.
brahmapuran:171:37	One who wishes to take wealth by gambling is deprived of dharma, wealth, desire and good birth, of manliness itself.
brahmapuran:171:38	Even in the Veda the act is condemned, which your father then took up. So what can we do, child? What has been told to you is to be done.
brahmapuran:171:39	What wise man transgresses the path ordained by the Creator?
Hearing the priest's words, Sumati said:
Doing what will my father Pramati regain the kingdom?
Again meditating, Madhuchchhandas said to Sumati:
Go to the Gautami, child; there worship Shankara, Aditi, Varuna and Vishnu; then he will be freed from the noose.
Saying "So be it," he quickly went, bowed to the Ganga and Janardana, worshipped Shambhu too and practised austerity with firm vows.
For a thousand years, he freed his bound father from the gods, and he regained the kingdom.
Freed from the noose by Shiva and Vishnu, he got the kingdom back from his own son; he obtained Gandharva knowledge and was dear to Shatakratu.
Shambhava, Vaishnava and also Urvashi-tirtha: from then on that holy place is famed as Kaitava.
What is not obtained by the grace of Shiva, Vishnu and the mother river? Bathing and giving there give much merit, release from the noose of sin and destroy all misfortune.
Seeing the teacher's most venerable (wife), Sindhu (the ocean) thought what to do: "She who is to be bowed to by the lords of the world, worshipped by Brahma, Isha and others —
I should go to meet her, lest there be a defect in dharma; he who out of delusion does not greet a great soul who arrives,
has no protector in either world, a sinner." Having considered thus, the jewel-lord, embodied and humble, with joined palms, the lord of rivers, said to the Ganga:

Let the water in Rasatala, on the earth, in the sky, enter me alone here; I shall say nothing.
brahmapuran:172:9	In me are jewels, nectar, mountains, Rakshasas and Asuras; all these and others terrible I bear.
brahmapuran:172:10	Within me Vishnu with Kamala sleeps always; there is nothing impossible for me in the moving and unmoving.
brahmapuran:172:11	One who, out of pride, does not rise before a great person arriving, fallen from dharma and the rest, attains hell.
brahmapuran:172:12	There is no distress for me bearing them, except for the defeat by Agastya; but you are superior to them by reverence, therefore I
brahmapuran:172:13	say, goddess Ganga: come to me in equality. I am not able to meet you in a single form, if in many ways.
brahmapuran:172:14	If you, goddess, will come to the confluence, I shall meet; not otherwise. Ganga, if you come in many ways, I shall consider it.
To him, the lord of waters, speaking thus, the Gautami Ganga, the goddess, said: "Do this word of mine.
The wives of the seven sages, led by Arundhati, together with their husbands, all bring here; then I
will become lesser and meet you." Saying "So be it," he brought her surrounded by the sages with their wives; the goddess was divided in seven ways; and this Gautami Ganga went sevenfold to the sea.
By the names of the seven sages there became seven Gangas. Bathing, giving, hearing, reciting and
remembering there with devotion grant all desires. There is no holy place in the three worlds greater than this ocean for removing sin, obtaining enjoyment and liberation, and delight of mind.
Another should be known as Vamadevi, the auspicious Gautami in the middle, another is remembered as Bharadvaji, and another Atreyi,
and Jamadagni's, thus named sevenfold. By all those sages, the great-souled ones desiring to sacrifice there,
a great session was completed by sages who had seen the far shore. In the meantime a powerful enemy of the gods arrived there,
famed as Vishvarupa, at the sages' session; having duly propitiated them by celibacy and austerity, he humbly asked all the sages in order:
Surely, sages, you can tell, by sacrifices or austerity, how, as I wish, for the sake of my well-being, I may have a mighty son, hard even for the gods to withstand.
There the greatly wise, great-minded Vishvamitra said:

By action, dear, various fruits are obtained; of the three causes, action is the first cause.
brahmapuran:173:11	Then the doer is the cause; then another is declared, the material and the seed; the wise do not know action (alone).
brahmapuran:173:12	Even when action is the cause and a complete cause is present, the fruit is seen as arising or not; therefore the fruit depends on action.
brahmapuran:173:13	Action too is to be known as twofold: what is being done and what is done. What is to be done is the means for what is being done.
brahmapuran:173:14	Their states are the cause both in the success of action; whatever the discerning creature intends as he performs the action,
brahmapuran:173:15	according to that intention the fruit is produced, it is said. If one performs action by rule but without intention,
brahmapuran:173:16	the fruit will differ, according to his state. Therefore austerity, vow, gift, chanting, sacrifice and other acts
brahmapuran:173:17	give fruit by intention in accordance with the action; therefore action gives fruit in accordance with intention.
brahmapuran:173:18	Intention is to be known as threefold: sattvic, rajasic and tamasic; the fruit follows the action.
brahmapuran:173:19	Varied is the standing of actions according to intention; therefore the discerning should form the intention according to his wish.
brahmapuran:173:20	Afterwards the action too is to be done; the giver of fruit too is of that kind; he gives fruit to the fruit-seekers when the fruit is under way.
brahmapuran:173:21	There is no agent of action there; one acts by nature; and that material and the rest, by differences of the qualities, sattva and others,
brahmapuran:173:22	begins from intention; so the fruit is obtained by intentions. And action is the cause of dharma, wealth, desire and liberation.
brahmapuran:173:23	Action abiding in intention may be the giver of liberation or the cause of bondage. Action in accordance with one's nature is for oneself here and hereafter.
brahmapuran:173:24	It quickly produces various fruits, following equanimity; this one object is seen to differ by intentions.
brahmapuran:173:25	It is done or enjoyed, so intention is distinguished. Do action according to intention and you will obtain what you wish.
Hearing the word of the wise sage Vishvamitra, having practised austerity for a long time, taking a tamasic intention,
Vishvarupa did a terrible act, frightening the gods; though constantly forbidden, while the chief sages looked on,
he did a fearful act according to his own anger, in a fearful fire-pit, in fearful fire,
meditating on a fearful Rudra-Purusha, dwelling in the cave of the heart. Seeing him thus performing austerity, a bodiless voice spoke:

Without the matted hair, himself, Vritra was not conquered. In vain would Vishvarupa offer himself into the fire.
brahmapuran:173:31	He would be Indra, Varuna and everything; giving up himself, he offered only matted locks, born of sin.
brahmapuran:173:32	Vritra is spoken of in the Veda, and he too was born of sin. Who knows the greatness of the terrible one, lord of the world?
brahmapuran:173:33	He creates all and yet is not touched by attachment. Having said so, the voice stopped, lords of sages.
Having bowed to Bhimeshvara they went each to his own hermitage. Vishvarupa, very terrible, of terrible deeds and form,
of terrible disposition, meditating on a terrible body, offered himself. Therefore the god is called Bhimeshvara in the Purana; bathing and giving there grant liberation, no doubt.

One who with devotion recites or hears this, Shiva in his terrible form here as lord of gods, famed in the world, remover of all sin, by taking refuge in the remembrance of his place gives liberation.
The Godavari, destroyer of the entire mass of sin, giver of the highest good, is always and everywhere so, but especially where she has entered the ocean.
The righteous embodied one who bathes at the confluence of the Godavari and the sea, lifting his forefathers from all the severe hells, goes to Shiva's city.
That Brahman, to be worshipped, knowable by the Vedanta, is directly Bhimanatha; when he is seen, embodied beings do not again enter the dreadful sorrow of worldly existence.

Sage, increasing the words with hymns by composers of mantras, Kashyapa, bow to Soma the king, who was born lord of plants.
brahmapuran:174:17	I am the poet, then the physician, the stone-grinder; with various minds, desiring wealth, we stood like cows (following).
Having said so, and having obtained soma for the thunderbolt-wielder, they gave it to him from the sages, and the sacrifice of Shatakratu was completed.
That is called Soma-tirtha; before it is the Agneya. Agni, having worshipped with great sacrifices and propitiated me, obtained what he desired.
By my grace he stays there constantly; for the benefit of the world Vishnu and Shiva too stay there.
Therefore it is called Agneya; next is the Aditya, where Aditya, made of the Vedas, constantly comes to worship,
in another form at midday, to see me, Shankara and Hari. There at midday every person should always bow.
In what form the Sun comes is uncertain; therefore it is called Aditya; next is the Barhaspatya.
From that holy place Brihaspati obtained worship by the gods and performed many sacrifices; hence they know it as Barhaspatya.
By mere remembrance of that holy place there will be peace of the planets. Another holy place beyond that, on the best mountain Indragopa,
a great linga was established for some reason by Himalaya; that holy place is called Adri-tirtha.
Bathing and giving there are auspicious and grant all desires. Thus the Gautami Ganga issued from Brahmagiri;
as far as the goddess goes to the sea, some holy places there have been told by me in brief, secret and auspicious.
The Gautami, famed in the Veda, Purana and among sages, bowed to by the world — who, Narada, has the power to tell of her of such great glory fully?
For one who acts with devotion in any way there is no offence, no doubt here; therefore after great effort she has been indicated only in outline for the good of the world.
Who is able to tell the greatness of each of her holy places? Even Vishnu, lord of Lakshmi, and Shiva Someshvara would not suffice.
Holy places somewhere become so at some time and conjunction; but the Gautami, greatly wise one, is always virtuous for men.
Holy everywhere and always — who can tell the praise of her virtues? Therefore "Salutation to her" alone is fitting.

I think there can be no holy place greater than her; no similarity with another holy place is fitting in any way.
brahmapuran:175:9	Having heard the praise of the Ganga's virtues through the nectar of my words, why did not the mind of all stop right there? So it seems wonderful to me, sage, in the three worlds.
brahmapuran:175:10	You are the knower and instructor of dharma, wealth, desire and liberation, of the Vedic metres with their secrets, and of the Puranas and Smritis too.
